examples.problem_statement:
Smoking is a known cause of certain serious health problems, including emphysema and lung cancer. Now, an additional concern can be added to the list of maladies caused by smoking. A recent study surveyed both smokers and nonsmokers, and found that smokers are significantly more anxious and nervous than nonsmokers. Which of the following is an assumption on which the argument rests?
(A) Anxiety and nervousness can lead to serious health problems.
(B) Anxiety and nervousness do not make individuals more likely to start smoking.
(C) Equivalent numbers of smokers and nonsmokers were surveyed for the study.
(D) Smokers are aware of the various health problems attributed to smoking, including lung cancer and emphysema.
(E) Smokers who had smoked a cigarette immediately before responding to the survey were more anxious and nervous than smokers who had not smoked for several hours.

solution.operation: Split the argument: premise = the survey shows smokers are more anxious than nonsmokers; conclusion = smoking causes anxiety and nervousness
solution.result: A premise that establishes only a correlation supporting a causal conclusion, A causes B
solution.description: Write the premise and the conclusion separately so the gap between them is visible: the study reports an association, while the conclusion asserts causation.

solution.operation: Apply the rule that an assumption behind a causal conclusion must protect the causal direction A \to B
solution.result: The needed assumption either rules out an alternate cause (C causes B) or rules out reversed causation (B causes A)
solution.description: Narrow the search to the two shapes an assumption can take in a causal argument, so the answer choices can be screened against them.

solution.operation: Test choice (B) by denying it: suppose anxiety and nervousness do make people more likely to start smoking
solution.result: Then B caused A, the anxiety preceded the smoking, and the conclusion that smoking causes the anxiety fails
solution.description: Negate the candidate and check whether the argument survives; here it collapses, which is exactly what marks (B) as a required assumption.

solution.operation: Check (A) and (D) against the conclusion's scope, which is only that smoking causes anxiety and nervousness
solution.result: Both are irrelevant: (A) concerns downstream effects of anxiety, (D) concerns smokers' awareness of health risks
solution.description: Discard choices that talk about consequences or beliefs the conclusion never claims anything about.

solution.operation: Check (C) and (E) against the same conclusion
solution.result: (C) is about the number of respondents, which the conclusion does not depend on; (E) compares some smokers to other smokers, a comparison the argument never makes
solution.description: Eliminate the remaining two by noting the mismatch between what each describes and what the argument actually rests on.

key_reminders: A survey showing that two things go together establishes correlation, not causation.
An assumption in a causal argument must preserve the direction of causation: it blocks either an alternate cause or the reverse direction.
A choice that lies outside the conclusion's scope cannot be a required assumption, however true it sounds.
common_mistakes: Choosing (A) by chaining anxiety onward to serious health problems, which strengthens the opening sentence rather than the argument's own conclusion.
Choosing (C) on the belief that a survey comparison needs equal group sizes, when the conclusion does not depend on the sample counts.
Missing the reverse-causation trap: anxious people may already be the ones who take up smoking.

concept.sub_category: Trains - two trains crossing each other

examples.problem_statement: The speeds of two trains are in the ratio 3 : 4. They are going in opposite directions along parallel tracks. If each takes 3 seconds to cross a telegraph post, find the time taken by the trains to cross each other completely?

solution.operation: Since each train crosses a telegraph post in the same 3 seconds, length = speed \times 3, so lengths are in the same ratio as speeds, 3 : 4
solution.result: Lengths can be written as 3x and 4x metres
solution.description: Convert the equal post-crossing times into a statement about lengths: with time fixed, length is proportional to speed, so the length ratio copies the speed ratio.

solution.operation: Recover the speeds from those lengths: \frac{3x}{3} and \frac{4x}{3}
solution.result: Speeds are x m/s and \frac{4x}{3} m/s
solution.description: Divide each assigned length by the 3-second post-crossing time to express both speeds in terms of the same x.

solution.operation: Because the trains move in opposite directions, add the speeds: x + \frac{4x}{3}
solution.description: Use the opposite-direction rule, where the speeds add, to get the single rate at which the gap between the trains closes.

solution.operation: Add the two lengths, since crossing completely means covering both: 3x + 4x
solution.description: Set the distance for a complete crossing equal to the sum of the two train lengths.
Apply time = distance / speed; the x cancels, so the unknown scale factor never has to be found.

solution.operation: Generalise with speed ratio a : b and lengths ax, bx: \frac{x(a+b)}{\frac{x(a+b)}{3}}
solution.result: 3 seconds for any ratio a : b
solution.description: Repeat the same division with a general ratio to see that the ratio cancels entirely, giving the quicker rule: when both trains take the same time to pass a post, they take that same time to cross each other.

key_reminders: Crossing a telegraph post means covering exactly the train's own length.
For a fixed crossing time, length is proportional to speed, so the length ratio equals the speed ratio.
Trains moving in opposite directions have relative speed equal to the sum of their speeds, and crossing each other means covering the sum of their lengths.
common_mistakes: Treating the 3 : 4 speed ratio as though the answer must depend on it, and hunting for a time other than 3 seconds.
Subtracting the speeds (the same-direction rule) instead of adding them for opposite directions.
Using only one train's length as the crossing distance rather than 3x + 4x.

examples.problem_statement:
The number line shows four positive variables ordered as 0 < a < b < c < d (the spacing shown is not stated to be even).
Quantity A: a \times c
Quantity B: b \times d
(A) Quantity A is greater.
(B) Quantity B is greater.
(C) The two quantities are equal.
(D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.operation: Record what the figure actually gives: 0 < a < b < c < d
solution.result: All four variables are positive and strictly increasing in that order
solution.description: Extract the only usable information, the ordering and positivity of the four variables.

solution.operation: Note what is not given: the exact values, and whether the variables are evenly spaced
solution.result: No numeric values may be assumed, and even spacing may not be inferred from the figure's appearance
solution.description: Guard against reading extra structure out of the picture, since a figure that looks evenly spaced is not stated to be.

solution.operation: Pair the factors and compare term by term: a < b and c < d, with all terms positive, so a \times c < b \times d
solution.description: Multiply the two smaller numbers against the two larger ones; positivity is what licenses multiplying the inequalities in the same direction.

solution.operation: Sanity-check with real numbers: a = 1, b = 2, c = 3, d = 4, then a = 0.5, b = 7, c = 11, d = 45
solution.result: 1 \times 3 < 2 \times 4 and 0.5 \times 11 < 7 \times 45, in both the evenly and unevenly spaced cases
solution.description: Plug in one evenly spaced set and one deliberately uneven set to confirm the ordering holds regardless of spacing.

solution.operation: Conclude from the general argument, which covers every scenario meeting 0 < a < b < c < d
solution.description: Since the comparison was proved for all admissible values rather than just the test cases, the relationship is determined and (D) is ruled out.

key_reminders: Inequalities between positive numbers may be multiplied term by term in the same direction.
Never assume a number line's tick marks are evenly spaced unless the problem says so.
'Cannot be determined' applies only when some admissible set of values flips the comparison.
common_mistakes: Choosing (D) because a, b, c, d have no numeric values, even though the ordering alone settles the comparison.
Assuming even spacing from the figure and reasoning about differences such as c - a versus d - b instead of the products.
Forgetting the positivity condition, which is what makes the term-by-term multiplication valid.
